blocks.text: What came back

slides.title: Measure the Attitude to Risk
slides.lead: Requirement: put a sure amount against a fair gamble and see which one the respondent takes, row by row.

blocks.text: Section 2, all eight rows exactly as asked

blocks.head: How it was done
blocks.body: The sure amount equals the gamble's average on every row, so one utility curve means the same side all eight times. We read the pattern of the picks.

blocks.head: How the step was completed
blocks.body: All four patterns were classified. 251250047 took the sure amount every time and 251250030 took the coin flip every time.

blocks.head: What it told us
blocks.body: 251250039 and 251250002 switch part way down, at rows 4 and 3, exactly as prospect theory predicts.

slides.title: Measure the Attitude to Waiting
slides.lead: Requirement: offer money now against more money later and find the return that makes waiting worthwhile.

blocks.text: Section 3, all six rows exactly as asked

blocks.head: How it was done
blocks.body: Each row implies a yearly return. The lowest offer waited for and the highest one turned down bracket the personal discount rate, and the midpoint of that bracket is the point estimate.

blocks.head: How the step was completed
blocks.body: A discount rate was produced for all four. 251250039 came out near 21.2% a year and 251250002 near 15.0%.

blocks.head: What it told us
blocks.body: Every rate sits above any return on offer, and 251250030 preferred cash at every rung. Worth a conversation about the real horizon.

slides.title: Fit the Utility Curve
slides.lead: Requirement: elicit a utility curve over wealth by the probability equivalence method from the lecture.

blocks.text: Section 5, with one respondent's own answers alongside

head: Item
Question on the form
251250039 said
rows: The lowest amount that feels relevant to you
The highest amount that feels relevant to you
Rs 30,000 for sure, or play the game. What winning chance makes the two feel the same?
Rs 40,000 for sure, or play the game. What winning chance makes the two feel the same?
Rs 45,000 for sure, or play the game. What winning chance makes the two feel the same?
Rs 47,999 for sure, or play the game. What winning chance makes the two feel the same?

blocks.head: How it was done
blocks.body: Set U(A) = 0 and U(B) = 1. At indifference the stated chance is the utility of the sure amount, so U(X) = p. Those points were fitted with a constant relative risk aversion curve by least squares.

blocks.text: The fitted curves
Both curves came out concave, so both respondents are risk averse: A = 0.66 and A = 1.18. That coefficient is the A used directly in Step 5.

slides.title: Fit the Value Function Over Gains and Losses
slides.lead: Requirement: measure how gains and losses are coded against a reference point, as prospect theory sets it out.

blocks.text: Section 6, all seven fields exactly as asked

head: Item
Question on the form
Answer scale
rows: The amount you measure gains and losses against
Win Rs 10,000 for sure, or play for Rs 20,000
Win Rs 20,000 for sure, or play for Rs 40,000
Win Rs 30,000 for sure, or play for Rs 60,000
Lose Rs 10,000 for sure, or risk losing Rs 20,000
Lose Rs 20,000 for sure, or risk losing Rs 40,000
Lose Rs 30,000 for sure, or risk losing Rs 60,000

blocks.head: How it was done
blocks.body: The gamble pays double or nothing, so v(X) = p times v(2X) at indifference. With v(x) = x to the power alpha the sure amount cancels and alpha is minus log base 2 of p.

blocks.text: The fitted parameters
All three gain rows measure the same curvature, so the spread between them is a direct read on how reliably the answer was given.

slides.title: Score the Personality Profile
slides.lead: Requirement: collect a standard personality measure so the advice can speak to behaviour, not only to risk.

blocks.text: Section 4, thirty short items, one sample from each domain

head: Domain
A sample item from the thirty
Scale
rows: Is compassionate, has a soft heart.
Is systematic, likes to keep things in order.
Is curious about many different things.

blocks.head: How it was done
blocks.body: Thirty items from the BFI-2, two per facet, chosen so all fifteen facets are covered within the thirty question cap. Reverse keyed items were flipped, facets averaged, domains averaged from their facets, then placed against the published norming means.

blocks.text: 1 means not like me at all and 5 means very much like me.

blocks.head: How the step was completed
blocks.body: All four answered all thirty items, so every domain and facet score is complete.

blocks.head: Output of this step
blocks.body: Five domain scores and fifteen facet scores per person.

slides.title: Build the Mean-Variance Portfolio
slides.lead: Requirement: combine the measured risk aversion with the Problem Statement 1 portfolio and set the equity weight.

blocks.text: The inputs, all carried forward rather than asked again

blocks.head: How it was done
blocks.body: Maximise U = E(r) minus half A sigma squared along the capital allocation line. The optimum is y* = [E(rP) minus rf] divided by A times sigmaP squared, capped at one because borrowing is not available.

blocks.text: Three return scenarios are carried through, because the expected return is the least certain input in the whole exercise.
The recommendation, base case inputs
Both respondents with a fitted curve want more than their whole corpus in the risky portfolio, so the cap sets the answer: hold 100%, which is Rs 90,000 and Rs 10 lakh.

slides.title: Build the Behavioral Portfolio
slides.lead: Requirement: go past mean-variance and size the layered portfolio that behavioral portfolio theory describes.

blocks.text: Section 7, the questions we added to the class form

head: Item
Question added to the form
What it measures
rows: A coin flip. Tails you lose Rs 10,000, heads you win G. How big must G be?
A 10 in 100 chance of Rs 10,000. What sure amount feels as good? Same at 90 in 100.
What is the smallest amount you must still have at the end?
How often could you live with falling below that amount?
What amount at the end would you call a success?
Split 100 points between staying safe and a real shot at the big number.
What would you give up to raise your chance of success by 10 points?

blocks.head: How it was done
blocks.body: Each layer needs one number the class form does not collect, so we wrote the seven shortest questions that supply them. They take about a minute to answer.

blocks.head: What the layered portfolio needs
blocks.body: A floor in rupees, a tolerance for breaching it, an aspiration level, and loss aversion. Together they split the corpus into a safety sleeve and a potential sleeve, each priced off the same frontier.

blocks.head: How it was completed
blocks.body: The engine, the estimators and the layer solver are built and tested, and all seven questions are live in the portal. The code path runs end to end on worked inputs.

blocks.head: The next pass
blocks.body: The four respondents answer the seven added questions, and the same run then prints a sized behavioral portfolio beside the mean-variance one.

slides.title: Turn the Numbers Into Advice
slides.lead: Requirement: write the commentary and the behavioral guidance that goes back to each respondent.

blocks.text: The rules, and the answer that triggers each one

head: Guidance
Fires when
Fired for
rows: Fix the review dates in advance
Step the equity weight up over time
Low negative emotionality and a long horizon
Show the downside in rupees, not percent
A switch part way down the risk ladder
Cash preferred at every rate offered

blocks.head: How it was done
blocks.body: Risk aversion is already measured in Step 4, so personality is used only where it predicts something else: whether the client stays with the plan. Each rule names the answer that set it off, so nothing in the advice is unexplained.

blocks.head: 251250039: build in the follow-through
blocks.body: Conscientiousness 2.33. Automate the contribution and rebalance on a threshold.

blocks.head: 251250047: methodical and calm
blocks.body: Conscientiousness 3.83 and the group's lowest negative emotionality at 1.67. A glide path suits this well.

blocks.head: 251250002: frame it in rupees
blocks.body: Balanced across every domain. The switch at row 3 suggests risk is judged in nominal amounts, so show the downside as a rupee figure.

blocks.head: 251250030: start with a conversation
blocks.body: Took the gamble throughout and preferred cash now at every rate. A short interview will establish the real horizon before the plan is set.

slides.title: What We Established, and What Comes Next

cards.b: Four respondents, so the conclusions are about the method rather than a population.
The least certain input, which is why three scenarios are carried through.
Single-period models, before contributions, taxes and costs.
Normality assumed, so tail figures are the optimistic end.
Current index membership, inherited from Problem Statement 1.

points: Every one of the six steps is traceable to the exact question that produced it, and every number in this deck is computed from a submitted answer.
Risk aversion is measured from the utility curve, and the ladder is read as the pattern it genuinely reveals.
Seven added questions complete the behavioral portfolio, and they are already live in the portal.
The next pass collects those answers and re-elicits two respondents, which closes out Steps 4 and 5 for the full group.
slides.quote: Measure what the data supports, and extend the instrument where it does not.
